chief_complaint: throbbing headaches at the back of the head and blurred vision for 3 weeks
hpi_details: 3-week history of severe, early-morning occipital throbbing headaches that gradually ease by mid-day. Over the past week, has experienced intermittent blurred vision, mild dizziness, and two episodes of nosebleeds (epistaxis). Stopped taking her prescribed blood pressure medication 6 months ago because she felt completely fine and disliked having to take daily pills.
ideas: thinks work stress and screen time are causing tension headaches and eye strain
concerns: worried she might be developing a brain tumour or having a stroke
expectations: wants strong migraine tablets and an eye check to clear her blurred vision
pmh: essential hypertension diagnosed 4 years ago, obesity (BMI 33)
medications: amlodipine 10mg OD (discontinued 6 months ago by patient), ibuprofen PRN for headaches
social_hx: non-smoker, zero alcohol, high-sodium diet (adds salt at table), bank manager

clinical_knowledge.topic: Severe Uncontrolled Hypertension with Target Organ Damage evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Severe Uncontrolled Hypertension with Target Organ Damage is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes assessing whether presentation constitutes hypertensive urgency versus emergency (if papilloedema, acute kidney injury, or encephalopathy is present, admit urgently for controlled reduction; in most hypertensive emergencies, lower mean arterial pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour, then toward 160/100-110 mmHg over the next 2-6 hours), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: throbbing headaches at the back of the head and blurred vision for 3 weeks

Key HPI features: 3-week history of severe, early-morning occipital throbbing headaches that gradually ease by mid-day. Over the past week, has experienced intermittent blurred vision, mild dizziness, and two episodes of nosebleeds (epistaxis). Stopped taking her prescribed blood pressure medication 6 months ago because she felt completely fine and disliked having to take daily pills.

Objective/Exam findings: Blood pressure: 196/114 mmHg in both arms after 5 mins rest. Fundoscopy: bilateral Grade III hypertensive retinopathy (flame-shaped retinal haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, copper-wiring, arteriovenous nicking; check for papilloedema). Dipstick urinalysis: proteinuria 2+ and microhaematuria. Bloods: U&Es (check creatinine for acute hypertensive nephrosclerosis), eGFR, FBC. 12-lead ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy (Sokolow-Lyon index).
Relevant background/PMH: essential hypertension diagnosed 4 years ago, obesity (BMI 33)
Current medications: amlodipine 10mg OD (discontinued 6 months ago by patient), ibuprofen PRN for headaches
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Severe Uncontrolled Hypertension with Target Organ Damage.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Primary hyperaldosteronism without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Headache with visual change, confusion, or chest pain — hypertensive emergency.
management_principles: Assess whether presentation constitutes hypertensive urgency versus emergency (if papilloedema, acute kidney injury, or encephalopathy is present, admit urgently for controlled reduction; in most hypertensive emergencies, lower mean arterial pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour, then toward 160/100-110 mmHg over the next 2-6 hours)
For severe asymptomatic hypertension after reassessment, restart long-term oral therapy with renal function and potassium monitoring
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 54F with non-compliant hypertension presents with 3-week occipital headaches, visual blurring, and epistaxis. No chest pain or dyspnoea.
reference_soap.objective: Blood pressure: 196/114 mmHg in both arms after 5 mins rest. Fundoscopy: bilateral Grade III hypertensive retinopathy (flame-shaped retinal haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, copper-wiring, arteriovenous nicking; check for papilloedema). Dipstick urinalysis: proteinuria 2+ and microhaematuria. Bloods: U&Es (check creatinine for acute hypertensive nephrosclerosis), eGFR, FBC. 12-lead ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy (Sokolow-Lyon index).
reference_soap.assessment: Severe uncontrolled essential hypertension with acute target organ damage (hypertensive retinopathy and nephropathy - Hypertensive Urgency/Emergency threshold). DDx: secondary hypertension (renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma), migraine with aura, intracranial space-occupying lesion.
reference_soap.plan: Assess whether presentation constitutes hypertensive urgency versus emergency. If papilloedema, acute kidney injury, or encephalopathy is present, admit urgently for controlled reduction; in most hypertensive emergencies, lower mean arterial pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour, then toward 160/100-110 mmHg over the next 2-6 hours. For severe asymptomatic hypertension after reassessment, restart long-term oral therapy with renal function and potassium monitoring. Counsel empathetically on the asymptomatic nature of hypertension and risks of stopping therapy. Dietitian referral for a low-sodium DASH diet.

learning_objectives: Distinguish hypertensive urgency from hypertensive emergency by assessing acute target organ damage (fundoscopy, urinalysis, ECG)
Explain why blood pressure must be lowered gradually in a hypertensive emergency rather than precipitously, to avoid organ hypoperfusion
Perform fundoscopic staging of hypertensive retinopathy (from arteriovenous nicking to papilloedema)
Address medication non-adherence in asymptomatic chronic disease through patient education and collaborative goal-setting

teaching.diagnosis: Severe Uncontrolled Hypertension with Target Organ Damage
teaching.one_liner: Blood pressure high enough for long enough to start damaging eyes, kidneys and heart — often silent until it isn't.
red_flags: Headache with visual change, confusion, or chest pain — hypertensive emergency

must_ask.say: Where is the headache, and is it worse in the morning?
Have you had any blurring of vision or spots in your sight?
What have your blood pressure readings been, and for how long has it been high?
Are you taking your blood pressure tablets every day?
How much salt and alcohol do you have, and do you take painkillers regularly?
Have you had any chest pain or breathlessness?
